messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Kofi

Kofi was twenty-one when three men assaulted him in the parking lot behind the restaurant where he worked as a sous chef. It was a Tuesday night in late autumn, just after closing. He had stayed behind to prep mise en place for the next morning's service—a routine that had made him feel competent, in control of at least one corner of his life. When he stepped outside to load his car, a group approached him with sudden aggression. What followed was a blur of fists, voices raised in anger, and a violation so complete that Kofi found himself unable to locate himself in his own body. The assault lasted perhaps ten minutes, though time had fractured in a way that made duration meaningless. What remained sharp was the sensation of powerlessness, the awareness that he could not stop what was happening, that his body was not his own.

In the weeks after, Kofi began to notice that his mind had split the experience into fragments he could not quite reassemble. When he tried to tell his sister what had happened, the words would scatter halfway through a sentence. He would start explaining the sequence of events and suddenly find himself unable to continue, as if the narrative itself had become too heavy to carry. Instead, he retreated into silence and into fantasies that felt more coherent than memory. In these fantasies, he was no longer the person who had been forced to the ground. He was someone who fought back, who overpowered the men, who made them understand the weight of what they had done. These imagined reversals occupied hours of his waking life, and though they brought a temporary sense of agency, they also left him feeling hollow afterward, ashamed of the violence he was rehearsing in his mind.

His body had become a source of constant vigilance. Kofi found himself checking his arms and torso throughout the day, running his hands across his skin as if searching for evidence of continued injury, as if the trauma might be visible in ways he had not yet discovered. At work, standing over the prep station, he would pause mid-chop to press his fingers against his ribs, assessing, monitoring, alert to sensations that might signal danger. His chef, noticing his distraction, had begun to question whether Kofi was still suited to the precision the kitchen demanded. A mistake with a knife—a slip that drew blood—sent Kofi into a state of panic so acute that he left the kitchen and did not return for three days.

The world had become a place of false threats. A car backfiring outside his apartment sent him diving behind the couch, heart hammering, convinced for several minutes that he was under attack. The sound of a car door slamming—a noise he heard constantly in the city—would trigger a cascade of physical alarm that his mind could not quite distinguish from genuine danger. Even at home, behind a locked door, he remained on high alert, his attention drawn to every shift in shadow, every unexpected sound. The sudden movement of a neighbor in his peripheral vision could trigger an immediate defensive crouch. His body was preparing for violence at all times, reading threat in the ordinary texture of daily life.

What frightened Kofi most was not the memories themselves, though they came without warning—a particular angle of light, a voice with a certain timbre, the smell of a cologne similar to one of the men—all of which could collapse him instantly back into that parking lot. What terrified him was the conviction that had taken root in the weeks since the assault: that he was fundamentally broken, that someone stronger, someone more like the person he had believed himself to be, would have prevented this from happening. He had come to believe that he had no future worth imagining, that the violation had erased something essential in him that could not be recovered. He had acted in ways that contradicted everything he understood about himself, and that contradiction had become a kind of living wound. When his mother asked when he would return to work, when friends suggested he should talk to someone, Kofi felt only the weight of their expectations and the certainty that he would disappoint them, just as he had disappointed himself. It was only after six weeks of increasing isolation, after his chef had finally said he could not hold his position any longer, that Kofi made an appointment with a therapist, driven less by hope than by the recognition that the life he had known was already gone.
